claims.text: The starting material is conventionally cast HfZrTiTa0.53.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a coarse and possibly heterogeneous microstructure.
The reported yield strength of HfZrTiTa0.53 is approximately 786 MPa.
The reported compressive strength of HfZrTiTa0.53 is approximately 1314 MPa.
The 13.5% reported terminal strain represents limited tensile ductility in HfZrTiTa0.53.
An 8–10% cold reduction followed by annealing at approximately 950°C for 1 hour with controlled cooling is an appropriate sub-transus thermomechanical treatment for HfZrTiTa0.53.
The proposed treatment will promote recrystallization in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The treatment will produce a refined, uniform, equiaxed grain structure and reduce residual stresses.
Cold reduction introduces dislocations that provide the driving force for fine-grained recrystallization during annealing.
A fine and uniform microstructure reduces stress concentrations and delays localized necking, thereby improving tensile ductility.
The treatment will leave the phase composition and strength-bearing features of HfZrTiTa0.53 largely intact.
Uniform tensile elongation will increase from approximately 13.5% to 20–27%.
The treated alloy will retain a yield strength of at least approximately 700 MPa.
The treated alloy will retain a compressive strength near 1300 MPa.
The treatment will not detrimentally affect impact-triggered energy release.
The proposed tensile-performance benefit applies at room temperature under quasi-static loading at approximately 5×10−4 s−1.
The treatment may produce different responses at elevated temperature or under high-strain-rate impact loading.
Treated and as-cast controls will be compared using matched room-temperature tension, compression, and impact tests.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant increase of at least approximately 20% over the 13.5% elongation baseline will falsify the hypothesis.
A greater than 10% decrease in yield strength, compressive strength, or impact energy release relative to the as-cast control will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is variously treated as terminal strain, a measure of limited tensile ductility, and the baseline uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain, fracture elongation, and uniform elongation are not interchangeable metrics, and the hypothesis does not establish that the reported value came from a tensile test.

The prediction requires no detrimental impact on energy release and strength preservation near the baseline, whereas the falsification rule permits decreases of up to 10% without falsification. Thus, the acceptance criterion is weaker than the stated preservation outcome.
